extracted.intended_audience: patent attorneys, inventors, and law students
extracted.subtask_description: Extracts legal standards under U.S. patent law for (1) the requirement of utility and its limits, and (2) abandonment (actual and constructive) including public-use/on-sale bars, laches, and experimental-use exceptions. Primarily doctrinal guidance for evaluating patent validity and prosecutorial risk.

rubrics_metrics.name: Utility — must perform specified function
rubrics_metrics.description: Utility is absent from all processes and devices which cannot be used to perform their specified functions, and patents for such subjects are therefore void.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a machine will not answer the purpose for which it was intended without some addition, adjustment, or alteration which the mechanic must introduce of his own invention (and which the patentee had not discovered when the patent issued), the patent is void (examples: Burrall v. Jewett; Bliss v. Brooklyn — inoperative/worthless couplings). A subsequent addition by others that makes a contrivance useful does not validate the original patent if the invention as patented was inoperative.

rubrics_metrics.name: Imperfect performance does not negate utility
rubrics_metrics.description: If an invention performs a good function, though imperfectly, its utility is not negatived by the fact that it is susceptible of improvement, or that some prior or later invention performs the same function as well or better.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Patents are not void merely because the invention operates poorly; limited commercial use means little public harm. Later superior inventions that supersede an earlier one do not invalidate the earlier patent for lack of utility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Utility may be satisfied by ornamentation (design utility)
rubrics_metrics.description: Utility in a manufacture is not negatived by the fact that it has no function except to decorate the object to which it is designed to be attached; in such cases utility resides in beauty.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aesthetic or decorative effect that gives pleasure is treated as a kind of utility (cases: Magic Ruffle Co. v. Douglas; Schultze v. Holtz). This supports patents on designs whose primary purpose is ornament.

rubrics_metrics.name: Utility negated if invention is injurious to morals, health, or good order
rubrics_metrics.description: Utility is negatived if the function performed by an invention is injurious to the morals, the health, or the good order of society (e.g., devices to facilitate forgery, spread contagious disease, or render air/water intoxicating).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts do not apply a pure balancing test (weighing good functions against evil) nor permit mere private opinion to control; instead the controlling standard is the average public sentiment of the time. Thus patents that are plainly designed to accomplish socially injurious ends will be unpatentable; borderline or contested moral issues are resolved by prevailing public sentiment (discussion includes Colt's revolver as an example).

rubrics_metrics.name: Utility negated when invention injures the thing to which it is applied or the machine as a whole
rubrics_metrics.description: Utility is negatived by the fact that the patented process or thing is injurious to the thing to which it is applicable, and also when a part's function, though good in itself, is injurious to the utility of the machine as a whole.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: a spark arrester that arrests sparks but so retards a locomotive as to make it impracticable was held lacking utility. The court looks to net utility in context of intended use.

rubrics_metrics.name: Patent as prima facie evidence of utility; estoppel from adoption
rubrics_metrics.description: A patent is prima facie evidence of utility, and doubts relevant to the question should be resolved against infringers; if the defendant has adopted the distinctive features of a patented device he is estopped to deny its utility.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because it is improbable people will risk infringement suits for useless features, courts start with a presumption of utility (cases cited: Vance v. Campbell; Crown Cork & Seal Co. v. Aluminum Stopper Co.). This shifts burden and weighs against attacking utility absent strong proof.

rubrics_metrics.name: Abandonment — actual vs. constructive (definitions)
rubrics_metrics.description: Abandonment of an invention may be actual or constructive. Actual abandonment results from the inventor's intention to relinquish all expectation of securing a patent; constructive abandonment arises from statute (e.g., public use or on-sale bars) regardless of intent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Either kind can occur before application or after application and before issue, and both are fatal to later patents. The inchoate right once abandoned cannot be resumed (gift to the public becomes absolute). The chapter treats the two types separately but notes common points of law and fact.

rubrics_metrics.name: Actual abandonment — proof standard and evidentiary forms
rubrics_metrics.description: Actual abandonment occurs when there is an entire relinquishment of all expectation of securing a patent and an accompanying formation of an expectation that the invention will always be free to the public. Such relinquishment may be shown by direct or circumstantial evidence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Burden of proof is on the party asserting abandonment and must be proven beyond a reasonable doubt. Acts or omissions (including delay to take legal steps) may establish abandonment, and abandonment may be shown even if it occurred within two years before the inventor later files an application to recall it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Express declaration/formal disclaimer/cancellation leads to abandonment
rubrics_metrics.description: An inventor abandons his invention when he makes an express declaration that it is open to anybody, or when he formally disclaims or cancels a claim in an application and substitutes no other claim for the same invention, or files a separate disclaimer paper.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A mere description in an application without claiming or disclaiming does not necessarily amount to abandonment; Supreme Court precedent holds description alone is not abandonment (examples: Battin v. Taggert; later reissue holdings). Formal acts of disclaimer or express dedication are decisive.

rubrics_metrics.name: Laches/delay can constitute actual abandonment; factors that may excuse delay
rubrics_metrics.description: Abandonment is also proved by evidence that the inventor is chargeable with laches or lack of diligence in applying for a patent. Long delay constitutes laches unless there was a reason rendering the delay consistent with expectation to secure a patent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Excuses that may negate laches include extreme poverty that prevented application, residence in the Confederacy during wartime, mental disorder or substantial physical incapacity, compelling working hours preventing timely consultation, delays caused by patent solicitor negligence, and delays caused by Patent Office slowness or by time allowed under statute or PTO rules. Delay caused by ongoing experiments may excuse some delay but not waiting indefinitely for accessory improvements once the idea is reduced to mechanical form. A delay intended to profit from secrecy until patenting (secrecy then filing to get monopoly) may constitute abandonment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Constructive abandonment — public use or on-sale bar (two-year rule)
rubrics_metrics.description: Under statute and precedent, a patent is void if the invention covered thereby was in public use or on sale earlier than two years before the application for that patent. The two years are measured backward from the date of filing the application (with certain rules where one application is withdrawn and another filed to replace it).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The two-year period may be measured from the first application if the later application was filed to replace a withdrawn one that described and claimed the same invention. An application that describes an invention takes the filing date even if it did not then claim the invention. Early statutes and decisions (Acts of 1836, 1839; Consolidated Act 1870) are cited for legislative history.

rubrics_metrics.name: Public use — definition and tests
rubrics_metrics.description: 'Public use' exists when the inventor allows his invention to be used by other persons generally (with or without compensation), or transfers the thing to a user without reserving control or expecting to change it. Use by the inventor for profit (not experimental) is public use.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Public use does not require more than one specimen or more than one person to know of it; ordinary uses that hide the article from view can still be public use. Exhibition of articles or pictures to make a design publicly known constitutes public use. Use by an inventor in the ordinary course of employment, where profit primarily goes to the employer, may still be public use.

rubrics_metrics.name: Experimental use exception — good-faith testing not public use
rubrics_metrics.description: Experimental use conducted in good faith for the purpose of testing the qualities of the invention is not public use within the statute, even if made openly, known to many, and continued for long periods, provided it is reasonably necessary to test or perfect the invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Experimental use becomes public use if it extends further in time or number of instances than reasonably required to test. For machines that manufacture articles, the inventor may make and even sell as many articles as necessary to observe and remedy defects and still not be charged with public use if the primary purpose was testing (cases: International Tooth Crown Co. v. Gaylord; Egbert v. Lippmann discussed). The line depends on purpose and scope of activity.
